title: Three-Pass Close Reading Protocol
preview: Students read a text three times with a different analytical lens each pass — gist, structure, and author's craft — building layered comprehension.

body.summary: A structured close reading protocol guiding students through three purposeful reads of a complex text, each with a distinct focus. The first read builds basic comprehension, the second analyzes structure and vocabulary, and the third examines author's craft and purpose. By the third pass, students have deep, layered understanding — not because the text was easy, but because they built meaning systematically.
body.whenToUse:
Use when introducing a complex or grade-level text that requires deep analysis. Ideal for:
• Anchor texts that will drive a unit
• Primary source documents
• Challenging informational passages with dense vocabulary
• Poems or literary excerpts with layers of meaning

Don't use for every text — save this for texts worth three reads. Simple or transparent texts don't need this level of analysis.
body.howToImplement:
FIRST READ — GIST (5-7 min):
1. Say: "Read the text all the way through. Don't stop to look up words. Just get the general idea."
2. When done, students write a 1-sentence gist statement: "This text is mostly about ___."
3. Quick share: 2-3 students read their gist aloud. Don't correct yet.

SECOND READ — STRUCTURE & VOCABULARY (8-10 min):
1. Say: "Now read it again. This time, circle words you don't know, underline key details, and put a star next to the main idea of each paragraph."
2. Students work with a partner to discuss: "What patterns do you see in how the author organized this? What words are essential to understand?"
3. Address 3-4 key vocabulary words as a class — use context clues first, then provide definitions.

THIRD READ — AUTHOR'S CRAFT (7-10 min):
1. Pose a focus question: "Why did the author write this? What is the author trying to make you think or feel?"
2. Students reread with this lens, annotating evidence of author's choices (word choice, tone, structure, rhetorical devices).
3. Class discussion: "What evidence supports your answer to the focus question?"

RESPONSE (5-8 min):
Students write a short analytical response using text evidence. Provide the frame: "The author's purpose is to ___. This is evident when the author ___ (cite specific text)."
body.teacherMoves:
IF students complain about reading it three times:
→ Say: "The first time you listen to a song, you hear the melody. The second time, you catch the lyrics. The third time, you notice the meaning. That's what we're doing with this text."
→ Make each pass feel different — change the task, change the grouping.

IF students can't write a gist statement after the first read:
→ Provide a frame: "This text is about ___ (topic). The author argues/explains/describes ___ (main point)."
→ Let students discuss with a partner for 30 seconds before writing.
→ Accept partial gist statements: "Even 'This is about the water cycle' is a start. We'll refine it."

IF students are not annotating during the second read:
→ Model annotation live: project the text and annotate the first paragraph together.
→ Give specific annotation targets: "Find at least 3 words you don't know and 2 key details."
→ Provide colored annotation guides: "Use blue for vocabulary, yellow for key ideas, pink for questions."

IF students struggle with author's craft questions:
→ Scaffold with multiple choice: "Do you think the author's purpose is to (A) inform, (B) persuade, or (C) entertain? Find one piece of evidence."
→ Give a word bank of craft terms: tone, word choice, repetition, imagery, figurative language.
→ Model: "Watch me find one example of author's craft in paragraph 1..."

IF the text is too hard for some students:
→ For the first read: provide an audio recording students can listen to while following along.
→ Chunk the text — do three passes on paragraphs 1-3 only, then move to 4-6.
→ Provide a brief summary of the text before the first read for Tier 2 students (this is not cheating — it's scaffolding).
body.variations:
TIER 1 (Core):
Use as described above. Vary the focus question for the third read based on the standard you're targeting.

TIER 2 (Scaffolded):
Provide annotation sentence frames for each pass:

First Read frames:
• "This text is mostly about ___."
• "I think the main idea is ___."

Second Read frames:
• "The word ___ probably means ___ because the text says ___."
• "This paragraph is mainly about ___."
• "A key detail that supports the main idea is ___."

Third Read frames:
• "The author uses ___ (technique) when they write '___' (quote). This makes the reader feel ___."
• "The author's purpose is to ___ because ___."

Pre-teach 2-3 critical vocabulary words before the first read. Provide a glossary for the second read.

TIER 2 (Alternative — Chunked Close Reading):
Instead of three passes through the whole text, break the text into 2-3 chunks. Do all three passes on Chunk 1 before moving to Chunk 2. This reduces cognitive load and keeps momentum.

ADVANCED EXTENSION:
After the three reads, students compare this text with a second text on the same topic. How do the authors differ in purpose, craft, or perspective? Write a comparison paragraph.
body.researchBase: Fisher and Frey (2012) demonstrate that repeated, purposeful readings significantly improve comprehension of complex texts, particularly when each read has a clear instructional purpose. The Common Core State Standards emphasize close reading as a foundational literacy practice. Shanahan (2012) notes that close reading is most effective when teachers resist the urge to pre-teach everything and instead let students build meaning through structured rereading.
